source_terms: The only way to come close to this in a still image is to arrange the framing, composition or lighting so that all the attention immediately goes to one place, but the eye lingers long enough on the frame to start to wander, and then discovers something else.

It’s an uncertain balancing act, because if you hide the thing-to-be-revealed too well, such as by making it too small or poorly lit, chances are the viewer will get bored and move on before noticing it.
item.claim: The reveal is a cinematic device — the camera shows one thing, then moves or zooms to disclose something else, effective through surprise — and the source says it is difficult and perhaps impossible to achieve in a single still. The only approach is to arrange framing, composition or lighting so that attention goes immediately to one place, but the eye lingers long enough to start wandering and then discovers something else. It is an uncertain balancing act: hide the thing to be revealed too well — too small, too poorly lit — and the viewer will get bored and move on before noticing it.

mechanism.text: In film the disclosure is controlled by the camera's movement. In a still it must be produced by the viewer's own scanning, so the photographer controls only how long the first subject holds and how findable the second is.

scope.conditions: a still image with a secondary subject intended to be found late

caveats.text: the source states the technique may be impossible in a still and then attempts it anyway — "But let's try anyway" — so the case is offered as an attempt rather than a demonstration
success and failure are described only in terms of the viewer's patience, and no way of testing whether the balance was struck is given

source_stated_problems: hiding the thing-to-be-revealed so well the viewer moves on before noticing it
source_stated_remedies: arrange framing, composition or lighting so attention goes to one place and then wanders

item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.source_locator: Ch. "Wide angle / short focal length", sub-headings "It's all about the context" and "Composition is the key" (spines 48-49)
item.question: A wide-angle landscape comes back looking empty, with the point of interest reduced to nothing. What does Carroll say happened, and what two devices does he prescribe?
item.answer: Shorter focal lengths seemingly elongate distance, so points of interest that looked relatively close to the naked eye become insignificant details lost within a wider composition. Wide-angle lenses create a lot of space in an image, so — his phrase — you really have to nail your composition. The two devices he names are leading lines and foreground interest, used to emphasise the focal points and pull the composition together. He also gives a second instruction for the near field: get close to your subject, and watch the periphery, because with a short focal length the edge detail plays an all-important role.
item.support: Wide angle spreads: wide-angle lenses cause periphery details to play an all-important role; shorter focal lengths seemingly elongate distance; points of interest become insignificant details lost within a wider composition; you really have to nail your composition; look for leading lines and foreground interest; make sure you get close to your subject.
confounders: reaching for a longer lens, which solves the emptiness but abandons the wide-angle picture
cropping in, which Carroll treats elsewhere as a fine tuner rather than a fix
assuming the problem is that the lens was too wide rather than that the composition was not built for the space

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces', the closing figure
item.question: The book says adding a three-dimensional object to a glossy flat surface both improves the picture and makes the lighting easier. Why does it help, and why does the chapter drop the idea immediately?
item.answer: It helps because the object's reflection in the surface is unambiguous evidence of gloss in a way that a featureless bright area is not: the reflection of a pair of eyeglasses in a polished lid tells the viewer the wood is glossy, and the authors say adding a secondary subject reveals the surface better than they are likely to render it alone. It makes the lighting easier for the same reason — the proof of the finish no longer has to be carried entirely by the shaped highlight. The chapter drops it because it had committed at the outset to two-dimensional and nearly two-dimensional subjects, and the authors say they cannot pursue the approach far without breaking that promise; three-dimensional subjects are the next chapter's business. So the claim is stated and demonstrated but deliberately not developed.
item.support: Ch. 4, 'Complex Surfaces', final paragraphs, with the eyeglasses-on-the-box frame.
confounders: reading the secondary object as a composition device rather than as evidence about the surface
assuming the book recommends it generally; it raises it and sets it aside for structural reasons
confusing it with camouflage on round metal, which hides an unwanted reflection rather than supplying a wanted one

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal, 'Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting' (spine 6)
item.question: Splicing and shifting move elements around. According to Samara, what is the actual payoff, and what does he tell the designer to do about it?
item.answer: The payoff is relational rather than formal. When information that would normally appear in its expected place — marking a structural juncture in the grid — is moved and lands beside some other kind of information, a new verbal connection is created that did not exist before. If a change in size or density accompanies the move, the shifted information may end up behind or on top of other material, and the resulting optical confusion will often make foreground and background appear to swap places. His instruction is telling: he says it is important to watch what happens. The connections are observed after the fact, not specified in advance.
item.support: "Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting": watching what happens when expected information is moved, the new verbal connection, and the foreground/background swap produced by optical confusion.
confounders: reading the operation as purely visual restructuring; Samara's stated payoff is a change in meaning
assuming the new connections are planned; his verb is 'watch'
confusing the figure-ground swap, presented here as a benefit, with the same effect treated as a hazard in the practicality section

source_terms: The action must be well lit so that it can be seen all the time; but in close shots the actors' faces should be the lightest spots on the screen.

(1) all lights are on; (2) no light moves; (3) dimmers are correct; (4) there is no voltage drop; (5) actors return to their designated positions (marks) exactly as in rehearsals; (6) one actor does not shade the face of another too extensively; (7) make-up was not damaged
item.claim: Lighting is finished in two passes with a rehearsal between them. The rehearsal is walked with the principals while stand-ins watch, and it exposes what the rough lighting missed — the source gives an example in which the faces went muddy as the actors crossed the set. Individual keylights are then added and balanced with kickers, with the rule that in close shots the faces should be the lightest spots on the screen. During the take seven specific things are checked, including that no light moves, that there is no voltage drop, that actors return exactly to their marks, and that one actor does not shade another's face.

scope.conditions: a shooting day on a lit set

caveats.text: the seven checks are physical-production conditions of the period; five of the seven have no counterpart outside a stage with electricians and actors

source_stated_problems: the general light was inadequate; the faces were underlit and consequently went muddy
source_stated_remedies: add individual keylights and balance them with kickers

provenance.section: The Theory of Illumination / Rehearsal, The Take

item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.source_locator: Ch. "Working the frame", sub-heading "Make every inch count" (spine 15)
item.question: Carroll's remedy for a composition that is not quite working is to change position "even very slightly". Why does such a small movement do anything at all, on his account?
item.answer: Because the elements in the frame do not move together. They lie at different distances from the camera, so as the camera shifts they move relative to one another at different rates. A small change of viewpoint therefore re-arranges the relationships inside the frame without changing the subject at all — which is why the instrument is a couple of steps rather than a different picture. His instruction is to change position slightly and keep an eye on how all the elements move around in relation to each other.
item.support: Working the frame spread: a little lower, a touch to the left, a couple of steps back; these minor adjustments make the fencepost vertical, frame the taxi rather than cut it in two, and ensure nothing is creeping into the frame; change position even very slightly and watch how the elements move in relation to each other.
confounders: explaining it as a change of perspective distortion or focal length; neither changes here
assuming the point is to find a better subject rather than a better arrangement of the same one
